---

## Overview

The goal is a general Python client library for calendaring **and task** data,
with a single clean API across many backends — CalDAV servers, JMAP servers,
local `.ics` files, read-only iCalendar feeds, and task/issue trackers.

### Guiding constraints

1. **Tasks should be first-class, not an afterthought.** iCalendar's `VTODO` is a weak
   task model — there is no agreed way to express a time estimate or time spent.
   The data model must be designed with real task trackers in view, not retrofitted.
   0.1 surveys that gap; 1.6 fills it.
2. **One API, honestly documented.** Backends differ enormously in capability. The
   library must not pretend otherwise. A published capability matrix (4.3) is a
   deliverable, not documentation garnish.
3. **Sync and async, from one source of truth.** Shipping a 2026 library without
   async is not defensible; shipping async-only is equally wrong, because sync code
   is far easier to write and to debug. The architecture must serve both without
   duplicating the implementation (0.2).
4. **Reuse, don't reinvent.** `caldav`, `icalendar`, `icalendar-searcher` and
   `recurring_ical_events` already exist and are maintained by the same group of
   authors, and `calendaring-jmap` is separately funded and under way.
5. **One protocol, one package.** Logic that is not CalDAV-protocol logic does not
   belong in the `caldav` library. This principle decides both the JMAP question
   and the shape of this project (see 0.3).

## Phase 0: Research and Design (44 hours)

### 0.1 Task and issue-tracker data model

- **Priority:** Critical — blocks 1.1
- **Estimated effort:** 20 hours
- **Deliverable:** a published analysis document, plus a proposed task data model
- **Dependencies:** none

The README's core complaint is that no good open standard for tasks exists. This
item establishes what a good model would have to contain, by surveying what real
systems actually do.

**Systems to survey:** Gitea, GitLab, Vikunja, Kanboard, EteSync, Taskwarrior,
Focalboard, OpenProject, Request Tracker, Emacs org-mode, and plain Markdown
task files.

For each system, record how it models — and whether it can round-trip:

**Tasks:**
- [x] Identity: is there a stable, client-assignable ID, or a server-assigned integer?
- [x] Time estimate and time spent — the gap the README names explicitly
- [x] Status lifecycle: is it a fixed enum, or user-definable per project/board?
- [x] Priority: numeric, ordinal, or a label?
- [x] Dates: due, start, scheduled, deferred — and which of them exist at all
- [x] Recurrence: supported, faked, or absent
- [x] Dependencies and parent/child relations
- [x] Assignment, ownership, and multi-user semantics
- [x] Labels/tags/categories, and whether they are free-form
- [x] Change detection: ETag, revision counter, `updated` timestamp, or nothing
- [x] Search and filter capabilities offered server-side
- [x] Auth model, pagination, and rate limiting (a real implementation cost)
- [x] Check what iCalendar already offers: RFC 9253 relationship support, and
      whether its `ESTIMATED-DURATION` (or any registered extension) closes the
      estimate gap, or whether an `X-` extension / native model is needed
- [x] Survey the `X-` properties already used in the wild for time tracking
      (Taskwarrior, org-mode exports, plann)
- [x] Publish the analysis, with a recommendation for the library's task model
- [x] Recommend which single tracker to implement first (feeds 2.5), with reasons

**Note on scope:** this is research plus a model proposal. Implementing a backend
is separately budgeted (2.5). Twenty hours across eleven systems is roughly 1.5 h
each plus write-up; that is enough for an informed survey, not for deep expertise
in any one of them.

---

### 0.2 Sync/async architecture

- **Priority:** Critical — blocks 1.1 and 1.3
- **Estimated effort:** 16 hours
- **Deliverable:** a published design document with a prototype-backed recommendation
- **Dependencies:** none

The caldav library reached its dual-mode design by accretion, and
[`ASYNC_DESIGN_CRITIQUE.md`](https://github.com/python-caldav/caldav/blob/master/docs/design/ASYNC_DESIGN_CRITIQUE.md)
documents the resulting failure modes: a forgotten `is_async_client` check silently
discards a coroutine with only an easily missed `RuntimeWarning`, the return type annotations lie,
and every new I/O method is a latent bug requiring three separate guards to be
correct. That history is the *reason* this item exists — a greenfield library with
no backward-compatibility obligation and no sunken cost in existing tests gets one
chance to choose better.

The partial Sans-I/O work in caldav succeeded at the protocol layer (pure XML
builders and parsers, testable without HTTP mocks) but was abandoned at the object
layer, because too many places in the old code did I/O unexpectedly. Whether that
was a property of Sans-I/O or a property of *retrofitting* Sans-I/O onto a
fifteen-year-old codebase is precisely the open question.

**Candidates to evaluate:**

| Approach | One source of truth? | Build step? | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| Runtime dual-mode (`if self.is_async_client`) | No | No | caldav 3.x; documented failure modes above |
| Separate async classes (motor / aiohttp pattern) | No | No | Correct types, but the I/O methods are written twice |
| Generator-based Sans-I/O (`yield request`, driver sends the response back) | **Yes** | No | Two thin drivers (~20 lines each); the h11 / hyper-h2 pattern |
| Async-first + code generation (`unasync`, AST transform) | Yes, in source | **Yes** | httpcore/urllib3 do this; cost is debuggability of generated code and stack traces |
| `greenlet` bridging (SQLAlchemy pattern) | Yes | No | Adds a C dependency; tracebacks are hard to follow |

**Tasks:**
- [x] Write up each candidate with its cost model
- [x] Prototype the two or three most promising against a toy two-method backend
- [x] Measure, for each prototype: implementation LoC, test LoC, whether one test
      suite can drive both modes, mypy/pyright correctness of the public signatures,
      traceback quality when a backend raises mid-operation
- [x] Answer explicitly: can the *object* layer be Sans-I/O without an ugly public
      API? A caller must be able to write `event.save()` or `await event.save()`,
      not `client.execute(event.build_save_request())`
- [x] Check how the chosen approach survives an HTTP-paginated backend (issue
      trackers) and a filesystem backend, not only a single-request-per-call one
- [x] Publish the comparison
- [x] The author's decision, recorded in the comparison's last section

**Explicitly rejected without further study:** wrapping async in `asyncio.run()` for
the sync path. Nested event loops are forbidden and it cannot be called from an
already-running loop.

**Note:** the author's stated position is that "write async, generate sync" is
unattractive. The generator-based Sans-I/O and greenlet options are the two that
give a single source of truth with no build step, and generator-based Sans-I/O is
the one that matches the instinct behind this item. The research must still be
allowed to reach a different conclusion.

It was given the chance: codegen (`unasync`) was prototyped too. Two candidates
hold up — generator-based Sans-I/O with typed façades (p2b) and async-first
source with a generated sync copy (p4) — and the prototypes do not settle which
serves the project better. The comparison sets out the trade without
recommending one; see [§10 of the comparison](SYNC_ASYNC_ARCHITECTURE.md#10-p2b-and-p4-compared).
The author chose p4, for its aesthetics and debuggability, despite the
reservation about generated code noted above; see
[§11](SYNC_ASYNC_ARCHITECTURE.md#11-decision).

**Note:** We should in general be careful relying too much on the
AI-generated code and documentation, but GenAI is great for rapid
prototyping.

### 0.3 Prior art, standards and project decisions

- **Priority:** High — blocks 1.1
- **Estimated effort:** 8 hours
- **Deliverable:** a short document recording each decision and its rationale —
  [`PRIOR_ART_AND_DECISIONS.md`](PRIOR_ART_AND_DECISIONS.md), which records the
  author's decisions of 2026-10-05
- **Dependencies:** none

**Tasks:**
- [x] **Settle the name.** `calendaring`, the same on GitHub, PyPI and as the
      import name (D2). It does not signal task support by itself; the
      tagline carries that. Free on PyPI as of 2026-10-05. (this decision may need
	  reversal, the rest of the team thinks it's not intuitive what a "calendaring"-
	  package is doing)
- [x] **Write up the packaging principle.** (D1) Two questions a reviewer will ask are
      already decided, and both follow from one principle: logic unrelated to the
      CalDAV protocol does not belong in the `caldav` library.
      - *This library is a separate package*, not a backend layer inside a
        hypothetical caldav v4. A multi-backend abstraction is by definition not
        CalDAV-protocol logic.
      - *JMAP lives in `calendaring-jmap`*, a separate package, separately funded by
        NLnet and under way. It is **not** part of this project's 248 hours. The
        `caldav/jmap/` module currently inside the caldav library is by the same
        principle misplaced; migrating it is caldav's and `calendaring-jmap`'s
        business, not this roadmap's.
      The work here is to record the principle and its consequences, not to decide
      them.
- [x] Review `icalcli`'s pluggable-backend design (already researched in an earlier README; see [PRIOR_ART_AND_DECISIONS §1.1](PRIOR_ART_AND_DECISIONS.md#11-icalcli))
- [x] Review how HomeAssistant currently handles calendar integrations, and whether
      this library is useful to them (README names them as a target user)
- [x] Standards review: RFC 5545 (iCalendar), RFC 5546 (iTIP), RFC 7265 (jCal),
      RFC 9253 (relationships), JMAP Calendars (RFC 8984 / JSCalendar), ActivityPub,
      org-mode. Record which are in scope for the funded period.
- [x] Record a Python version support floor and a typing strictness policy:
      `>=3.11` (D4), `mypy --strict` plus `pyright --verifytypes` (D5)

## Phase 1: Framework (68 hours)

### 1.1 Unified API design and peer review

- **Priority:** Critical
- **Estimated effort:** 20 hours
- **Dependencies:** 0.1, 0.2, 0.3
- **Deliverable:** a documented API specification, peer-reviewed —
  [API_DESIGN.md](API_DESIGN.md) (drafted 2026-10-08; peer-reviewed in [PR 5](https://github.com/pycalendar/calendaring/pull/5) and in video calls, 2026-10-10 – 2026-10-13)

The API should feel familiar to caldav users without being a CalDAV API in
disguise. The test of the design is not "does it fit CalDAV" but "does it fit
CalDAV *and* a Gitea issue tracker without lying about either".

**Tasks:**
- [x] Define the object model: workspace, backend, collection, calendar object,
      task, event, journal
- [x] Define the search/filter interface, reusing `icalendar-searcher` so that
      client-side and server-side filtering behave identically
- [x] Define the capability-declaration mechanism: how a caller asks a backend
      what it can do, and what happens when it asks for something unsupported
      (raise, degrade, or emulate client-side — and how the caller chooses)
- [x] Define error taxonomy and the exception hierarchy
- [x] Define change detection across backends with no ETag (mtime, revision
      counters, or nothing)
- [x] Define the escape hatch: how a caller reaches backend-specific functionality
      without the abstraction pretending it does not exist
- [x] Incorporate the task model from 0.1; fields with no standard property
      are stored as `X-` properties (0.3, D6)
- [x] Peer review, and revise. Identify and approach reviewers early — a review
      is a dependency on someone else's calendar, not a quantity of work.

### 1.2 Abstract base classes and the backend conformance suite

- **Priority:** Critical
- **Estimated effort:** 14 hours
- **Dependencies:** 1.1
- **Deliverable:** ABCs plus an executable conformance suite —
  `calendaring.testing` (`AsyncConformance` / `SyncConformance`), the ABCs in
  `src/calendaring/_async/`, and the in-memory reference backend
  `calendaring.memory` (drafted 2026-10-14)

The conformance suite is the load-bearing piece of this project: **one test suite
that every backend must pass**, parameterised by declared capability. It is what
makes "the same API regardless of backend" a checkable claim rather than a promise,
and it is what makes each later backend cheap to add.

**Tasks:**
- [x] Write the conformance tests first, against the API spec, before any ABC exists
- [x] Confirm the tests fail (there is nothing to run them against yet)
- [x] Define the abstract base classes the tests imply
- [x] Make the suite capability-aware: a backend declares what it supports, and
      unsupported operations are asserted to fail in the specified way rather than
      being skipped silently
- [x] Make the suite run in both sync and async mode, per 0.2's conclusion
- [x] Build an in-memory reference backend so the suite has something to pass

Notes from doing it:

- The suite is written once, async, and the sync suite is generated from it
  like the library code. That needed 1.3's generator early, so
  `tools/generate_sync.py` and its freshness test came with this item; the
  rest of 1.3 (type-checker gate, specimens, replacement-map hardening,
  contributor documentation) is still open. One finding for 1.3 already:
  unasync's output depends on the Python version. From 3.12 (PEP 701) an
  f-string is tokenised into parts and names inside its expressions are
  renamed; on 3.11 it is one token and they are not. A test now rejects a
  name to be renamed inside an f-string in `_async/`.
- The reference backend takes a capability profile, and four profiles run
  the suite: `FULL`, `TRACKER` (tasks only, mapped status and priority,
  assigned UIDs), `MINIMAL` (writable, most optional features left out, no
  collections of its own, so the suite borrows one that already holds an
  item) and `FEED` (read-only). Three more in the test module (events
  only, tasks without a status, and a feed of tasks) reach the branches
  these four left out, which a review found
  ([issue 21](https://github.com/pycalendar/calendaring/issues/21)); CI
  fails below 95 % branch coverage of the suite. The supported branches of
  `recurrence.edit-occurrence`, `recurrence.edit-this-and-future` and
  `task.complete-recurring` (below) are still not run. Every skip says why:
  a write test on the read-only profile after the write was checked to
  raise, or a recurrence test where nothing recurs.
- A backend implements a handful of primitives (`_query`, `_fetch`,
  `_create`, `_update`, `_delete`); capability checks, loss policies,
  client-side filtering, change emulation, `move` emulation, `relatives` and
  `verify` are written once in the base class.
- Two features were added to [§5.1](API_DESIGN.md#51-the-table):
  `recurrence.edit-occurrence` (saving one occurrence) and
  `task.complete-recurring`. Every backend, CalDAV included, declares
  both `UNSUPPORTED` until
  [edit-icalendar](https://github.com/pycalendar/edit-icalendar) has them
  ([API_DESIGN Q3](API_DESIGN.md#10-open-questions)).
- Sorting reads `icalendar_searcher.Searcher._sort_keys`, a private
  attribute; `test_search_sorts` catches a rename, and a public accessor
  belongs in icalendar-searcher.
- `save()` always writes, as Q13 decided on 2026-10-15. The tracked
  `component` subclass it had decided before would have waited for
  [icalendar issue 1914](https://github.com/collective/icalendar/issues/1914).

### 1.3 Sync/async scaffolding

- **Priority:** Critical
- **Estimated effort:** 10 hours
- **Dependencies:** 0.2, 1.1
- **Deliverable:** the chosen architecture, implemented and enforced

**Tasks:**
- [x] Before implementing: a clean-context review of 0.2's `unasync` prototype
      (p4) and the claims made for it
- [x] Implement 0.2's decision (p4) as reusable scaffolding: async-first
      source in `_async/`, a recursive generator that writes `_sync/` and
      deletes orphans, and a freshness test that compares file sets as well
      as contents; per-mode code in a hand-written layer underneath
- [x] Decide between depending on `unasync` and vendoring an equivalent
- [x] Maintain the generator's replacement map for names that must not follow
      the `Async*` → `Sync*` rename, such as unprefixed public sync classes
- [x] Gate CI on pyright, or mypy with `check_untyped_defs`, over both copies,
      plus ruff F841, with a test that the checker flags a committed specimen;
      run the conformance suite under `-W error`
- [x] Check that `_async/` contains nothing a token rewrite breaks (`asyncio`,
      third-party `Async*` names, `await(...)`)
- [x] Make dev-only tools fail the build when missing in CI rather than skip
- [x] Ensure the public type signatures are correct under mypy in **both** modes —
      the caldav failure was annotations that lie — and gate CI on a test that
      the checker catches a missing and a spurious `await` (0.2's three cases)
- [x] Document the pattern for contributors adding a backend

Enforcement is not optional; it is the whole point of the item.

Notes from doing it:

- The generator, its freshness test and the per-mode layer
  (`_concurrency.py`) came with 1.2.  This item added the enforcement
  around them: `tests/test_enforcement.py` runs mypy and ruff, with the
  project's own configuration, over the planted mistakes in
  `tests/specimens/` and asserts that exactly the marked lines are
  flagged, in both modes.  The correct calls in the same files are 0.2's
  case 1, for the main entry points (`open`, `collection`, `save`,
  `complete`, `tasks`, `iter_search`, `search`).  The shapes the checkers miss, such as a missing `await` in a
  comprehension, are planted unmarked, so a checker that starts or stops
  catching one fails the test.  The plain `mypy` and `ruff check .` runs
  exclude the specimens.
- mypy `strict` implies `check_untyped_defs`.  The specimen's unannotated
  method is the test that it is in effect.  pyright is not run: mypy
  already flags every shape pyright does in 0.2's table.
- `-W error` was already in `filterwarnings`.  A test now runs pytest with
  the project's configuration on an async test that drops a coroutine,
  and asserts that the test fails.
- **unasync stays a dependency, pinned exactly**, rather than vendored.
  Against it: four years between 0.5 and 0.6, `import setuptools` at
  import time, and output that depends on the Python version for
  f-strings (1.2's note).  Vendoring would remove the setuptools import
  and nothing else, at the price of owning a token rewrite.  Each of its
  quirks now has a test (f-strings, `aclose`, `await(...)`, third-party
  `Async*` names), the output is committed, so users never install it,
  and the pin makes every contributor generate the same bytes.  Revisit
  if a new Python breaks it.  The CI matrix runs the freshness test on
  every supported version.
- The replacement map is checked from both ends.  A generated class may
  keep the `Sync` prefix only if it is a bound item or `SyncConformance`,
  and an entry no `_async/` source uses any more fails the build.
- A missing dev tool fails the tests that need it rather than skipping
  them.  `test_generated_sync.py` imports unasync, and
  `test_enforcement.py` refuses a missing mypy or ruff.
- CONTRIBUTING.md documents the rules for `_async/` and the steps for
  adding a backend.

### 1.6 Time-tracking model and API

- **Priority:** High
- **Estimated effort:** 12 hours
- **Dependencies:** 0.1, 1.1
- **Deliverable:** a time-tracking data model and the public API over it
- **Downstream consumer:** `plann` Phase 4 (18 h), which is budgeted on the
  assumption that this exists

**This is not 0.1.**  0.1 is the survey: it asks how eleven real systems represent a
time estimate and time spent, whether RFC 9253 or `ESTIMATED-DURATION` closes the
gap, and which `X-` properties are already used in the wild by Taskwarrior, org-mode
and plann.  It produces a recommendation.  This item builds the thing 0.1
recommends, and puts an API on it.  The split is the same one as 0.1 → 2.5: research
in Phase 0, implementation in the phase that owns the code.

It is a separate item rather than part of 1.1 because it has a committed downstream
consumer with its own funded hours.  `plann`'s roadmap item 4.1 specifies
`complete --spent/--log/--start/--end` "writing through the library's time-tracking
API", and 4.2's `sum_hours` aggregates what this model stores.  Those 18 hours are
funded in the `plann` grant on the assumption that this API exists; these 12 hours
were moved out of that grant for the same reason (see the note in the MoU).  It
therefore must not be trimmed, and it must land before `plann` reaches its Phase 4.

**Tasks:**
- [x] Implement the model 0.1 recommends: estimate, spent, and the relationship
      between them
- [x] Decide and document the iCalendar representation, including whether an `X-`
      property is used and under whose namespace — iCalendar has no standard answer,
      and whatever is chosen here is what other tools will have to read
- [x] Time spent is an append-only log with the total derived — settled by 0.1
      ([survey 3.2](TASK_MODEL_SURVEY.md#32-dimension-by-dimension)). What
      remains is what round-trips through a backend that stores only the total
- [x] The API: start, stop, log a duration after the fact, amend, and read back
- [ ] Map it onto each backend's native notion where one exists (task trackers
      generally have one; CalDAV does not), and declare the capability honestly
      where it does not — the capability and the hooks are in, and CalDAV
      (2.1) declares it; a tracker's own log is 2.5's
- [x] Extend the conformance suite (1.2) to cover it, including the lossy cases
- [x] Aggregation primitives sufficient for `plann`'s `sum_hours` — grouping a
      selection into budget lines with per-line subtotals, keeping committed and
      spent time separate
- [x] Coordinate the design with `plann` before freezing it; a review of how
      the design affects `plann` is cheap now and expensive after 1.0

Notes from doing it:

- The design is "Time tracking" in [API_DESIGN §3.4](API_DESIGN.md#34-task).
  It was reviewed by plann's author in three rounds.  His comments
  changed who did the work from `ORGANIZER` to RFC 9073 `PARTICIPANT`,
  and cut the planned `X-` properties from five to two
  (`X-PYCAL-TIME-ENTRY`, `X-PYCAL-TIMER-START`).  plann's earlier design
  notes (a `VJOURNAL` per entry) were set aside: a `VJOURNAL` holds no
  interval.
- Time is logged against events as well as tasks (time spent in a
  meeting), so the methods are on every bound item.
- Research during the review overturned an assumption of the survey: the
  trackers it took for total-only (GitLab, Request Tracker, Kanboard,
  OpenProject, Gitea) mostly keep individual entries, and what they lack is
  the start time.  So `time-log` is `LOSSY` with `details["lost"]` naming
  the missing fields; `total-only` is the exception.
- Two fake backends in `tests/_async/test_memory_conformance.py`, a
  tracker's own log without start times and a total-only one, run the
  lossy branches until 2.5 brings real ones.
- The 2.1 backend declares `time-log` `FULL` on a server caldav has hints
  for (the conformance suite checks the `PARTICIPANT` component on
  Xandikos and Radicale), `UNKNOWN` on another, and `UNSUPPORTED` in a
  calendar holding no events, where `time_log_collection` points elsewhere.

## Phase 2: Backends (62 hours)

Each backend is "done" when it passes the conformance suite (1.2) in both sync and
async mode, and its capability declaration is accurate.

### 2.1 CalDAV backend

- **Priority:** Critical
- **Estimated effort:** 16 hours
- **Dependencies:** 1.2, 1.3

Thin in principle — it wraps the caldav library — but the mapping work is real,
and this is the backend that will expose every place the unified API and CalDAV
disagree.

**Tasks:**
- [x] Map the unified API onto `caldav` 3.x
- [x] Map caldav's compatibility-hint/quirk system onto the capability declaration
- [x] Handle the sync/async impedance between caldav's dual-mode design and
      p4 as 1.3 builds it — this is the interesting part, and the part most likely
      to overrun. caldav's `Async*` names are aliases of its dual-mode classes,
      so a thin, honestly typed shim is needed for type checking to work in
      this layer at all (see 0.2's comparison, *What is not settled*), and
      every caldav name needs a replacement-map entry so the generated sync
      layer imports names that exist (`SyncDAVClient` does not)
- [x] Settle [API_DESIGN Q12](API_DESIGN.md#10-open-questions) (`delete()` on an
      occurrence, and conflicts between sibling occurrences) before mapping
      `delete()` and `save()` for occurrences
- [x] Tune `verify=True`'s comparison against what real servers rewrite
      (parameter quoting, split `CATEGORIES`, TZID to UTC), and compare
      subcomponents such as `VALARM` too; it compares raw unfolded lines today
      (roadmap 1.2 review)
- [x] Decide what `get(uid)` returns for a stored object holding several
      overrides and no master; it returns the first today (roadmap 1.2 review)
- [x] Pass the conformance suite
- [x] Record, do not silently fix, bugs found in `caldav` itself: those fixes are
      caldav's budget, not this project's
      ([caldav #797](https://github.com/python-caldav/caldav/issues/797), its test
      servers; the occurrence-deletion plan is on
      [#598](https://github.com/python-caldav/caldav/issues/598))

---

### 2.2 Local iCalendar file backend

- **Priority:** High
- **Estimated effort:** 14 hours
- **Dependencies:** 1.2, 1.3

The README promises that the API works identically against local files and remote
servers. That promise is what makes this more than a `glob()` call.

**Tasks:**
- [x] Support both layouts: one directory of `.ics` files, and a single file
      (and a root directory of vdir collections, as vdirsyncer writes them)
- [x] UID-to-filename mapping, including collisions and unsafe characters
- [x] Atomic writes and file locking (a lock only for the single file, whose
      writes are a read-modify-write of the whole file)
- [x] An ETag surrogate (mtime and/or content hash) for collision detection
- [x] A sync-token surrogate for change detection
- [x] Search via `icalendar-searcher`, so filtering behaves as it does server-side
- [x] Full CRUD, passing the conformance suite.  Occurrence edits and
      recurring-task completion stay `UNSUPPORTED` until
      [edit-icalendar](https://github.com/pycalendar/edit-icalendar) has
      them (API_DESIGN Q3)

---

### 2.3 iCalendar feed backend (read-only HTTP)

- **Priority:** High
- **Estimated effort:** 6 hours
- **Dependencies:** 1.2, 1.3, 2.2

The best value-per-hour item in the roadmap: a long-standing user request that was
rejected as out of scope for the caldav library, and cheap here because
`icalendar-searcher` already provides the filtering and 2.2 already provides the
parsing.

**Tasks:**
- [ ] Fetch and parse a remote `.ics` URL
- [ ] Detect whether a URL is a feed or a CalDAV endpoint
- [ ] HTTP caching: `ETag` / `If-None-Match`, `Last-Modified`, and honour
      `REFRESH-INTERVAL` (RFC 7986) where present
- [ ] Declare read-only capability honestly, so writes fail as specified
- [ ] Pass the read-only subset of the conformance suite

---

### 2.4 JMAP backend

- **Priority:** Medium
- **Estimated effort:** 14 hours
- **Dependencies:** 1.2, 1.3, and a usable `calendaring-jmap`
- **External dependency:** `calendaring-jmap`, a separately NLnet-funded sibling
  project. See the scheduling risk below.

Fourteen hours buys the *backend*, not the JMAP protocol implementation — that
happens in `calendaring-jmap`, on its own budget. The estimate is unchanged from
when the package's location was still an open question, because the cost here is
dominated by model mapping and conformance work rather than by how clean the
wrapped API turns out to be.

**Tasks:**
- [ ] Wrap `calendaring-jmap` behind the unified API, as an optional extra:
      it is AGPL, so a program that includes it must be conveyed under AGPL
      terms as a whole, which the docs must say (0.3, D3)
- [ ] Map JSCalendar objects to the unified model
- [ ] Pass the conformance suite against Stalwart
- [ ] Verify Cyrus's JMAP calendar coverage before promising compliance against it;
      if it is partial, document the gap rather than working around it
- [ ] Declare capabilities accurately, including anything JMAP does that CalDAV
      cannot

---

### 2.5 First task-tracker backend

- **Priority:** High
- **Estimated effort:** 12 hours
- **Dependencies:** 0.1, 1.2, 1.3
- **Deliverable:** one working task backend, chosen in 0.1

This is where the abstraction is proved or disproved. If the unified API cannot
express this backend without contortion, the finding is more valuable than the code.

**Tasks:**
- [ ] Implement the tracker recommended by 0.1
- [ ] Run Gitea as a CI service container (official image, SQLite) for the
      conformance suite; a permanent instance is optional, for dogfooding
- [ ] Auth, pagination and rate limiting for that tracker's API
- [ ] Map its task model to the library's, and record every lossy mapping
- [ ] Let the write primitives apply [API_DESIGN §3.5](API_DESIGN.md#35-native-passthrough)'s
      native-value rule: `_create`/`_update` get only a calendar today, and
      `complete()` drops `native_status` through `as_data()`; add a
      conformance test that an unchanged save keeps the native value
      (roadmap 1.2 review)
- [ ] Report unknown IANA properties and subcomponents as losses where
      `properties.passthrough` is `UNSUPPORTED`; only `X-` properties are
      today (roadmap 1.2 review)
- [ ] Pass the conformance suite, with unsupported operations failing as specified
- [ ] Write up what did not fit — this feeds the capability matrix (4.3) and any
      later API revision

GitHub is the next tracker after this one, even though it is not funded (see
[Beyond the funded scope](#beyond-the-funded-scope)). 0.1 did not survey it.

### 3.2 CalDAV server compatibility

- **Priority:** Medium
- **Estimated effort:** 8 hours
- **Dependencies:** 2.1

The caldav project already maintains docker-compose test infrastructure for eleven
servers (Baïkal, Bedework, CCS, Cyrus, DAViCal, Davis, Nextcloud, Open-Xchange,
SOGo, Stalwart, Zimbra). This item **reuses** that infrastructure rather than
rebuilding it, which is why 8 hours is plausible where a from-scratch effort would
be four times that.

**Tasks:**
- [x] Run this library's conformance suite through the existing docker test servers
      (`pytest --caldav-servers=...`), along with readable scenario tests;
      run on Baikal and SOGo so far
- [ ] Confirm the capability declarations match observed behaviour per server
- [ ] File server-specific divergences as issues; fixing quirks in the caldav
      library is caldav's budget
- [ ] If the target is a specific server count, name the servers — the existing
      infrastructure covers eleven, and each addition costs real hours

### 3.3 Dogfooding: `plann`

- **Priority:** High
- **Estimated effort:** 6 hours
- **Dependencies:** 2.1, and ideally 2.5

The strongest available evidence that the API design works. `plann` is a real

**Tasks:**
- [ ] Port a meaningful subset of `plann` onto this library
- [ ] Record every place the unified API was harder to use than caldav's

- **Priority:** Critical

The most-cited document this project will produce, and the mitigation for the

Distinct from 4.4.  4.4 is *peer review*: recruiting outside readers, collecting what

## Risks

### The abstraction collapses into a lowest common denominator

CalDAV, an `.ics` feed and a Gitea issue tracker have little in common. A unified
API over all three risks being either too thin to be useful — every real caller
reaching for a backend-specific escape hatch — or leaky enough that it lies about
what backends can do.

**Mitigation:** the capability declaration (1.1) and the capability matrix (4.3)
are design constraints from day one, not documentation written at the end. The
conformance suite (1.2) is capability-aware, so "this backend cannot do X" is an
asserted, tested fact rather than a skipped test.

### The task model does not survive contact with a real tracker

**Mitigation:** 0.1 runs before the API is designed, and 2.5 implements a real
tracker before 1.0. If the model fails, it fails at hour ~175, not hour ~245.

### The sync/async decision is wrong

If the chosen architecture turns out unworkable during Phase 2, the cost is a
rewrite of the scaffolding and every backend's I/O path.

**Mitigation:** 0.2 prototypes rather than reasons in the abstract, and 2.1 — the
backend most likely to expose the problem, because it must bridge to caldav's own
dual-mode design — is the first one implemented.

### Recurrence editing depends on edit-icalendar, which has no code yet

Occurrence edits, "this and future" and recurring-task completion all go to
[edit-icalendar](https://github.com/pycalendar/edit-icalendar)
([API_DESIGN Q3](API_DESIGN.md#10-open-questions)). As of 2026-10-25 it has
a README and no code, no item of this roadmap schedules it, and its design
is still open ([edit-icalendar issue 3](https://github.com/pycalendar/edit-icalendar/issues/3)).
Until it lands, `task.complete()` on a recurring task raises on every
backend, which hits plann's everyday "complete" on a recurring task
(3.3).

**Mitigation:** the features are declared `UNSUPPORTED`, so callers can
check before calling. On CalDAV the escape hatch keeps caldav's completion
available ([API_DESIGN §3.7](API_DESIGN.md#37-recurrence)); the plann port
uses it ([plann issue 55](https://github.com/pycalendar/plann/issues/55)).

### 2.4 depends on a sibling project that does not exist yet

`calendaring-jmap` is separately funded and under way, but this roadmap cannot
control its schedule. If it is not usable by the time Phase 2 reaches it, 2.4 stalls.

**Mitigation:** 2.4 sits late in Phase 2 and is one of the two designated release
valves (with 2.5). The conformance suite (1.2) means the backend can be written
against the sibling package's API as soon as that API is settled, rather than
waiting for the package to be complete. If the slip is severe, the 14 hours move to
2.5 or to Phase 3 and JMAP lands in a later release — the release plan already
isolates it in 0.3.0.

### Maintainer bandwidth

The primary maintainer has a lot of packages to juggle, both packages
funded by NLNet and other packages - as well as other priorities and
concerns in life.  It's a real risk that time will run out before the
allocated funds run out.

It's important to be aware that the *number of calendaring packages*
is a deliberate consequence of the packaging principle rather than
accidental sprawl.  Theoretically we could have launched a
pycal-package "doing everything calendar-related".  Maintaining five
packages instead of one monolithic package does involve some more
overhead and worries - but we believe it's better for the community to
have small and dedicated packages doing one job right, rather than a
big monolithic monster-package.

**Mitigation**:
* There are more developers in the pyorg-pool, so other people may pick up bits and pieces if the primary maintainer won't have sufficient time for it.
* Getting this project out is a priority for the maintainer, if he has to priority it's more likely that the funding for the many of the less important features in the CalDAV project will discarded.

### Peer review is a dependency on other people

Two items (1.1, 4.4) require external reviewers, and a third (4.5) is carried
out entirely by a named outside contributor.

**Mitigation:** approach reviewers during Phase 0, not when the work is ready.

## Beyond the funded scope

Everything below is in the README's ambition but **outside the 248 funded hours**.  The maintainer has a vision to continue maintenance and development of the project with or without funding, though the first priorities will always be to get food on the table.

| Item | Rough estimate | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Mobilizon backend, bidirectional | 40–60 h | README calls this "quite high on my list"; federated event distribution, ActivityPub-based |
| iTIP over email: sending `.ics` attachments | 16–24 h | RFC 5546; the sending half is much cheaper than the receiving half |
| Mailbox access via IMAP and/or JMAP mail | 32–48 h | Reading invitations out of a mailbox; a different problem from calendar access |
| GitHub issues backend | 12–16 h | **First priority after 2.5**, funded or not: the project's own issues live on GitHub. Proprietary and not self-hostable, so CI runs against recorded responses or a dedicated test repository. Issues are REST; Projects v2 fields (status, estimates) are GraphQL-only. No estimate, time log or priority on an issue, so it tests the capability declaration much as Gitea does |
| Additional task-tracker backends | 12–20 h each | After 2.5 the marginal cost drops, but auth and pagination are per-tracker |
| Emacs org-mode backend | 24–32 h | Parsing org is its own project; a subset may be tractable |
| Plain Markdown task files | 8–16 h | Depends entirely on how much convention is assumed |
| jCal (RFC 7265) and xCal (RFC 6321) representations | 16–24 h | Format work, not backend work |
| Proprietary systems | unbounded | README's position: pull requests welcome, no effort committed |
| Completing the `plann` migration | 24–40 h | 3.3 buys evidence; this buys the migration |
| `vobject` and `ical` representations | unknown | Conversion helpers, and borrowing another library's object (lend it out, parse it back on exit; not the change tracking of API_DESIGN Q13). Raw data in and out (`from_ical()`, `to_ical()`, `replace_ical()`) is in the funded API; see [API_DESIGN, Raw data and other libraries](API_DESIGN.md#raw-data-and-other-libraries). Mentioned so that it is not added ad hoc |
| Save if edited | 4–8 h | `save()` skips an item nobody edited, sparing the round trip, the new `etag` that makes other clients download it again, and a needless `ConflictError`. Needs a check whether the item changed; the simplest compares `to_ical()` with the serialisation taken when the item was read, at one extra serialisation per read ([API_DESIGN §12](API_DESIGN.md#12-beyond-the-funded-scope-implicit-synchronization)), or `icalendar` may offer one ([icalendar#1922](https://github.com/collective/icalendar/issues/1922)). Whether skipping becomes the default or an opt-in, and whether `wire=` and `overwrite=True` always write, is part of the work. The funded `save()` always writes ([API_DESIGN Q13](API_DESIGN.md#10-open-questions)) |
| Implicit synchronization | unknown | Edits reach the backends without an explicit `save()`; write strategies and transactions, [API_DESIGN §12](API_DESIGN.md#12-beyond-the-funded-scope-implicit-synchronization). Agreed in the [PR 5 video meeting](https://github.com/pycalendar/calendaring/pull/5#issuecomment-6122366863): wanted, but not a priority. The funded API keeps `save()` and `reload()` explicit. Needs a check whether a component changed, which may need enhancements in `icalendar`; the discussion in [icalendar#1922](https://github.com/collective/icalendar/issues/1922) now proposes a check against a deep-copied snapshot (`was_modified_since()`, not implemented yet) rather than change notification; a yes/no answer is enough |
